rationale: The original review preview separates the list of Parkinson symptoms from its botanical inventory. The bibliography includes isolated crocin in a depression-like Parkinson mouse model and separate motor comparisons. An attributable ground saffron comparison on clinical Parkinson depression cannot be resolved from the preview.

The University of L'Aquila record authenticates the article and lists a 1.54 MB publisher PDF restricted to authorized users. The author abstract covers saffron compounds, Parkinson and depression among different contexts. The Wiley abstract and reference display leave the study-level exposure and depression comparisons open.

The original structured abstract reports 64 directly included records from a search through April 30, 2024. The displayed references include a saffron-versus-sertraline depression trial outside Parkinson and a separate Alzheimer's trial. The author-upload listing offers a request route and the public publisher preview leaves the exact Parkinson-depression study tables unavailable.

The original Tables 1–3 separate the Jin chronic-stress rat depression study from the Wang 6-OHDA Parkinson rat study. Jin measured depressive-like behavior with isolated rosmarinic acid. Wang measured striatal dopamine and dopaminergic neuron preservation. Table 3's human row concerns high-rosmarinic spearmint and knee osteoarthritis. These comparisons supply constituent and model context for fresh rosemary.

The original preview lists insomnia in Parkinson background and Crocus sativus in a separate herbal inventory. The available paper segments do not isolate a ground saffron Parkinson insomnia result or confirm how the review distinguishes sleep quality and insomnia severity.

The original Table III places ginger-containing foods and drinks under nausea management for dopamine agonists. Table IV lists oral ginger for nausea and identifies the evidential basis as expert opinion without published data. Dyskinesia belongs to the drug comparisons. This is a clinical review of a genuine ginger lead for a different outcome.

The original review preview names rigidity in Parkinson background. The displayed saffron fly citation concerns locomotor climbing and the identified human crocin source reports a motor total. The complete review still needs a check for a separately reported rigidity item with clinically relevant culinary exposure.

The preview lists fatigue as a symptom and saffron as a reviewed botanical in separate material. No preparation-specific Parkinson fatigue comparison is attributable from the preview, the verified references or the public author record.

The primary publisher and PubMed identify Part II as the Alzheimer review and Part I as the separate Parkinson review. The abstract lists fatigue as broad background and Crocus among plant sources. The exact author PDF listing was found, but the public route inspected supplied no readable PDF for Part II.

The official Hebrew record and PubMed English abstract place cranberry under urinary infection prevention, acupuncture under depression and tai chi under Parkinson. The original Hebrew download page displays access options and supplies no public full narrative. No dried cranberry depression measure appears in either abstract.

The original publisher sections identify dried ginger rhizome as laboratory starting material and seven isolated analytes tested in an artificial membrane permeability assay. The verified conclusion identifies three passive-permeability compounds. Animal anxiety and Parkinson studies occur in the introduction as previous work. The measured outcome is membrane diffusion in this experiment.

The original publisher introduction discusses customary tea use for tiredness. An original methods excerpt identifies the PINK1 fly experiment and the results excerpt compares fly locomotor capacity. The test compound is EGCG and the outcomes are locomotion, neuronal and metabolic readouts. This is a related constituent model with no clinical brewed tea fatigue estimate in the inspected sections.
